citations.quote: Conceptual design plays an important role in the space product development process. The model-based concept framework rooted in design theory contains information about key entries that should be taken into account during the early design phase.

We showcase this process by applying the proposed framework to a CubeSat swarm mission to detect gamma-ray bursts. The software developed as part of this case not only allows to determine the mass, power, and cost budgets but also provides estimates for such ADCS performance indicators as detumbling time, pointing and attitude determination accuracy. Informed by this data, the ADCS designer is then able to determine if the chosen architectural solution meets the requirements.

Another utility of the proposed framework is that it facilitates the ADCS development in the Concurrent Engineering Design environment by identifying functional interactions between the ADCS and its surrounding systems - other CubeSat subsystems - and thus informing the data flow between the corresponding design teams. To support this flow, the software developed has the capability to produce various attitude-specific data relevant to other subsystems.

Several years ago, a consortium has been formed comprising several Russian technical universities with the aim to incorporate skills and knowledge possessed by its members to build a set of small spacecraft to demonstrate algorithms of swarm behavior. Skoltech joined the consortium to offer its competence in systems engineering and concurrent design and become an integrating party putting together the parts of the project done by other universities [6]. The mission objective, in addition to swarm technology demonstration, was suggested by the colleagues from Moscow State University: their gamma-ray detectors can be used on several satellites flying in a group to track Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) or Terrestrial Gamma-Ray Flashes (TGFs) and calculate their sources' coordinates by means of triangulation. The detectors, previously flown on small satellites, are perfect to be mounted on CubeSats, of which there has to be at least three in order to be able to calculate the coordinates of an incoming gamma burst.

Thus a number of studies has been carried out with the aim of designing the spacecraft themselves [6] and their ADCS in particular [7], [8]. This paper reflects the results of these studies and generalizes them by proposing a procedure to apply a model-based conceptual design approach to ADCS development.

In our paper we use the system concept representation framework [12] that serves as a tool for the ADCS concepts development and analysis at the conceptual design phase. Throughout a paper, we use the notation of the Object-Process Methodology [13].

The information about 28 entries spread among 5 propositions is required to specify the alternative concepts and the decomposition of each one of them. The detailed rationale to include each one of these entries into the system concept representation framework has been provided in [12].

Applying the system concept representation framework to the ADCS system concepts development we start with the identification of stakeholders and their needs. In this article, as an illustrative example, we identify the stakeholders as the "mission control team" (entry 1), whose need is "CubeSat attitude state" (entry 2) - see Figure 2. After this we formulate the solution-neutral problem (entries 3-7).

Once this information is defined, the system architect can further execute the conceptual design, defining the specialized operand, specialized process, and finally - assigning the instrument to the function. The specialized operand of "spacecraft" is "CubeSat" (entry 8), the specialized processes of "handling" are "controlling" (entry 11.1) (CubeSat's attitude state, entry 9.1) and "determining" (entry 11.2) (CubeSat's data, entry 9.2). Note that the attributes (entries 10A, 10B, and 10C) are inherited from the solution-neutral environment. The core essence of the conceptual design is its ability to capture the form that executes the function.

ADCS concepts were developed down to the third level of decomposition, separately for systems with and without MSD. The second-level decomposition diagrams of ADCS form and function are shown in Figures 3 and 4 respectively. Due to the similarities between MSD and non-MSD systems, both types are presented within the same diagrams - MSD systems contain all the elements of non-MSD systems plus additional elements, which are filled with orange colour in the diagrams. The data flow between the processes is shown in Figure 5. Table 1 associates each of the processes (elements of function) with its respective instruments and operands (elements of form).
011 - Powering unit (part of ADCS hardware - for example, part of the ADCS board) powers the subsystem, including its computing unit, sensors and actuators.

As one can see from the diagrams, there is no significant architectural difference between MSD and non-MSD systems, which sits in accordance with the empirically established impression of those system types. Hence, the same framework (presented in Table 1) can be used for representing both types of ADCS with simply setting some of the elements/processes (the ones associated with the MSD state monitoring and MSD desaturation) of the framework to null when describing systems without MSD.

The architectural differences between ADCS for different missions first appear at the third level of decomposition. To illustrate this, Figure 6 shows a second-level OPM diagram for the 'Attitude State Determining' process on the left and its generic thirdlevel representation on the right. An example of the same process representation for a specific mission is shown in Figure 7 where the diagram depicts the elements and processes of the swarm mission CubeSat ADCS. As one can see from the diagrams, the differences between ADCS for different missions are encoded by decomposing generic objects (such as Sensors, SR Routines, AD Routines, Interfacing Unit), their data attributes (such as Sensor Data, Extended Attitude State Data), and the corresponding generic processes (Sensing, Sensors Reading & Pre-Processing, Sensor Data Processing) into their specific components and specifying the respective connection links between those.

For example, the swarm mission ADCS (see Figure 7) uses a magnetometer (Magn), a gyro (G), six Sun sensors (Sun S1, ..., Sun S6) and two Earth sensors (Earth S1, Earth S2). The sensors, by interacting with the environment (Earth's magnetic field, Sun, Earth) or being affected by the motion of the CubeSat (in case of the gyro), produce 10 sets of raw data (RD1...RD10) recorded in each of the sensors. To obtain this data from the sensors, the respective sensor reading and preprocessing routines (M SSR, G SSR, SS1 SSR ... SS6 SSR, ES1 SSR, ES2 SSR) are used. The routines are supported by the I2C data interface (in case of the swarm mission, all sensors are connected to the main computing unit via the same interface).

The proposed framework can be used as an instrument to describe different CubeSat ADCS concepts in a uniform and formalized way. In this capacity, it can serve as a basis for developing tools supporting the ADCS design team participating in concurrent design sessions.

At present, the framework is being used to develop a concurrent design tool that would provide the ADCS design team with quick rough estimations of the system performance based on the architectural decisions they make while exploring possible ADCS solutions for a specific mission. At this stage, the main components of the prospective tool have been outlined, and an Excelbased prototype of the tool was created to validate the core ideas to be implemented in the tool. The swarm mission ADCS design process was simulated to test the mockup.

The prototype includes the following components: parametric models of the main ADCS components (each parametric model is a row in the table), including: - Attitude Maneuver Computing Routines library (at this stage, the Excel mockup does not include components unique for ADCS with MSD): each routine is characterized by the Extended Attitude State Data it takes as its input, types of actuators it computes actuations for, and an approximate number of math operations; each routine is also associated with some control parameters (which are accessible to the user through the front-end interface - see examples below) and functions that implement formulas assessing the system performance;

- Sensors library: the main characteristics of each sensor are the type of Sensor Data it provides and its raw accuracy; at this stage, it is assumed that each sensor has only one SRRP Routine, and it is described in the corresponding sensor model as having a certain number of operations and providing a certain SRPP accuracy (derived from the sensor raw accuracy); the sensor model also includes the corresponding electric characteristics, data interface type, and mass (future versions of the library will also include sensor cost estimations); - Actuators library: each actuator is characterized by its type, 'main performance parameter' (g.e., by magnetic moment for magnetorquers), the characteristic number of math operations for the corresponding AR and AA routines, electric parameters, data interface (if any), and mass (future versions of the library will also include actuator cost estimations); - The fifth library containing parametric models of the integrated Computing, Powering, and Interfacing Unit is to be added to the tool in the future. It is assumed that the contents of the five libraries will accumulate gradually over time, as the Skoltech ADCS team works on its projects; at this stage, the libraries include the components of the swarm mission CubeSat ADCS as well as some mockup models for testing; - an Excel VBA module containing functions that emulate approximation formulas.

citations.quote: ADCS design process is modeled in the tool as a sequence of decisions made by the design team for each of the ADCS modes being explored. Though the set of decisions is the same for each mission and each ADCS mode, the specific options for those decisions are dependent on the options selected during the previous steps (for example, if the AD Routine chosen for some mode assumes using only magnetic field vector as its input, then only one of the sensor drop-down lists will be available to the designer at the next decision step, and this list will be populated with magnetometer models). Most of the work with the tool involves selecting options from drop-down lists. As soon as all the decisions are made, the designer is presented with performance and interface summaries for each of the modes and for the whole system.

- Step 0. Based on the mission information, define the list of attitude maneuvers that the ADCS shall be able to implement. For example, the swarm mission CubeSat ADCS shall be able to implement the following maneuvers derived from the general mission requirements: - Detumbling: decreasing angular velocity from some initial $ \omega_{0\mathrm{max}}=1 0 \mathrm{~d e g / s} $ to an acceptable value $ \omega_{\mathrm{a c c} \mathrm{m a x}}=1 \mathrm{~d e g / s} $

- Step 1. Start a new ADCS mode by entering its name in the corresponding field. - Step 2. Select the attitude control algorithm (AMC Routine) to use for the maneuver from the dropdown list. - Step 3. Select the attitude determination algorithm (AD Routine) for the selected attitude control algorithm from the drop-down list (the contents of the list will depend on the Step 2 choice). If there's more than one attitude determination algorithm needed for the maneuver (for example, an algorithm using Sun sensors for the day part of the orbit, and some other algorithm for the night part of the orbit), create an additional ADCS mode for each of the AD algorithms to be used and repeat the same steps for each of the modes created.

- Step 4. Fill in the Maneuver Parameters fields, if there are any (the list of parameters is different for different control algorithms). - Step 5. Select actuators. The number of active drop-down lists and their contents depend on the Step 2 Choice. - Step 6. Select sensors. The number of active drop down lists and their contents depend on the Step 3 Choice.

After identifying each of the ADCS modes, check if there are any modes that fully repeat each other consider merging them under a common name. Based on the selections made, the model will automatically compute the expected system performance characteristics and the respective summaries (see Figures 10, 11 for illustration). Presented with this information, the ADCS designer is able to determine if the chosen architectural solution meets the requirements.

The future work includes running of a number of concurrent engineering design sessions together with industrial partners. Another direction of future work includes the integration of DSM-based tools [14] to represent the specialization and decomposition relationships for alternative ADCS concepts.
